source.title: Defining Z in Q
source.version: Published article, Ann. of Math. 183 (2016) 73–93 (21 pages), read completely; arXiv:1011.3424v2 collated where noted. Locators are journal pages.
readSections: 2026-09-29: the published article, all 21 pages (§§1–4 and references), read completely; arXiv:1011.3424v2 (sha256 6f10efdd…) collated at the finding locators.
Poonen, arXiv:math/0703907v1, §4 read to identify the formula that Step 1 simplifies.

2026-09-30, FIX-RT-PAPER-KOENIGSMANN-16 (Codex, codex-rtOQ9t): targeted reread of published pp. 73, 78, 88, 90–92; page images checked for the two new misprints on pp. 90–91; arXiv v2 pp. 20–21 collated. Supplemental CTVG v1 Theorem 4.3 and MRS v3 Definition 2.2, Proposition 2.3(1), Lemmas 4.1–4.5 checked; hashes and exact scope in the fixes report. This is not a fresh full-paper read.

summary: Koenigsmann proves that Z is definable in Q by a universal first-order formula (Theorem 1), so Q \ Z is diophantine and Th_∀∃(Q) is undecidable, and gives an ∀∃-definition with one universal quantifier. The proof refines Poonen's quaternion-trace sets T_{a,b} = ∩_{p∈Δ_{a,b}} Z_(p), uses quadratic reciprocity to single out each Z_(p) by rings R^{[k]}_p, R^{[1]}_{p,q} chosen by the class of p mod 8, defines the Jacobson radicals of these semilocal rings existentially, and turns existential definitions of J(R) into universal definitions of R. It also shows that non-squares and non-norms from quadratic fields are diophantine by elementary means, and records closure properties of models of Th(Q). Tau Ceti already has weak approximation, and the atlas plans the other arithmetic inputs (Hilbert symbols, reciprocity, quaternion splitting, Hasse–Minkowski) and MRDP; the definability results themselves, with §4's consequences of Theorem 1, are routed to LogicAndDefinabilityInNumberTheory LD.4, and the general preservation criterion of §4 to LD.0. Confirmed red-team fixes add the model-completeness foundations at LD.0, itemize the external non-n-th-power theorem and local square input, and give ring-general Diophantine foundations and transfer a single owner at LD.4 shared with the ABS extraction.

items.name: First-order ring language and definable subsets of Q
items.statement: Mathlib provides the first-order ring language L_ring = {+, ·; 0, 1}, formulas, definable sets with a specified parameter set, and the syntactic classes of existential and universal bounded formulas. Applied to Q, these are the logical carriers used by the paper; identification with polynomial Diophantine definitions is a separate arithmetic interface.
items.note: Library status covers only the listed logical carriers. Use item 46 for the single ring-general finite-polynomial-system definition and item 42 for the Q-specific equivalence with existential ring formulas (including clearing rational denominators). No second Q-only Diophantine-set carrier is planned. LD.0 supplies logical syntax; LD.4 owns the polynomial interface.

items.name: Matiyasevich (MRDP): the existential theory of Z is undecidable
items.statement: Every recursively enumerable subset of Zⁿ is diophantine in Z; in particular Th_∃(Z) (and Hilbert's tenth problem over Z) is undecidable.
items.locator: §1, p. 73; used for Corollary 3 and Remark 24 and in Proposition 23(d)
items.note: Mathlib 082e2d3 has the hardest step of MRDP, that exponentiation is Diophantine over ℕ (Dioph.pow_dioph, from Pell.matiyasevic), but not the theorem that every recursively enumerable set is Diophantine; the item stays planned at LD.4.

items.name: Quadratic reciprocity with its supplements
Dirichlet's theorem on primes in progressions (used to choose auxiliary primes)
items.statement: For coprime a, m there are infinitely many primes p ≡ a (mod m); used to choose primes q ≡ 3 mod 8 with prescribed Legendre symbols modulo finitely many primes (Corollary 11, Lemma 20, Proposition 21(b)).

items.name: Lagrange's four-square theorem
items.statement: Every nonnegative rational is a sum of four rational squares; used to neutralise the factors a + Σxᵢ² and b + Σxᵢ² of the Step 1 polynomial when a ≤ 0 or b ≤ 0.

items.name: The semilocal rings Z_(p), Jacobson radicals and quaternion algebras
items.statement: Z_(p) = Z_p ∩ Q, the localisation of Z at p, with residue map φ_p; the Jacobson radical J(R) of a ring; the quaternion algebra H_{a,b} = Q⟨α, β⟩/(α² = a, β² = b, αβ = −βα).
items.note: Mathlib's QuaternionAlgebra R a b c has i² = a + b·i and j² = c, so Koenigsmann's H_{a,b} is QuaternionAlgebra ℚ a 0 b (notation ℍ[ℚ, a, b]). Z_(p) is the localisation of Z at the prime ideal (p), a subring of Q only after the IsLocalization identification. Tau Ceti already packages the reduced norm and its diagonalization as QuaternionAlgebra.normForm and QuaternionAlgebra.equivalent_normForm_weightedSumSquares; reuse them for item 16.

items.name: Local splitting of quaternion algebras and the norm criterion
items.statement: For a, b ∈ Q^×, the set Δ_{a,b} of places where H_{a,b} does not split is finite, and Δ_{a,b} = ∅ iff a is a norm from Q(√b) (a ∈ N(b)); p ∈ Δ_{a,b} iff the Hilbert symbol (a, b)_p = −1.
items.note: The reviewed AUDIT-05 marks QuadraticFormInvariants Layer 2 partly built: the quaternion norm form and several explicit split cases exist, while the general four-fold splitting criterion and split-or-division dichotomy remain planned. This item does not claim those conclusions from the norm-form API alone.

items.name: Explicit Hilbert symbols of Q (Observation 5)
items.statement: For odd p, a = p^α u, b = p^β v with u, v units: (a, b)_p = (−1)^{αβ(p−1)/2}(u/p)^β(v/p)^α; for p = 2: (a, b)_2 = (−1)^{ε(u)ε(v) + αω(v) + βω(u)} with ε(u) = (u−1)/2, ω(u) = (u²−1)/8 mod 2; for p = ∞: (a,b)_∞ = −1 iff a < 0 and b < 0. Equivalently p ∈ Δ_{a,b} exactly in the listed cases; at 2 the 16 pairs of square classes listed in Observation 5 (verified here: they are exactly the pairs with (a,b)_2 = −1).
items.note: QuadraticFormInvariants 6C supplies the finite-place formulas (odd residue characteristic, the Q_2 formula and its 8-by-8 square-class table). The p = infinity clause is owned by GlobalQuadraticForms Layer 4.4, which proves the real and complex symbol computations separately because 6C carries nonarchimedean hypotheses. CA.1 records residue-symbol interfaces only.

items.name: Hilbert reciprocity
items.note: QuadraticFormInvariants 6C item 14 exports hilbertSymbol_productFormula (from ClassFieldTheory.hilbertProductFormula), and GlobalQuadraticForms 4.4 proves the localized product formula; either gives the product over all places of ℚ.

items.name: Hasse–Minkowski for representations, and the Hasse norm theorem for quadratic fields
items.statement: A nondegenerate quadratic form over Q represents c ∈ Q iff it does over every Q_p and R; in particular x ∈ S_{a,b}(Q) iff x ∈ S_{a,b}(Q_p) for all p ∈ Δ_{a,b} (Fact (e)), and c ∈ N(b) iff c is a local norm everywhere.
items.note: Representation (Fact (e)) is GlobalQuadraticForms 6.1; the norm half (Proposition 21(e)) is its 4.3 quadratic Hasse norm adapter, which consumes Class Field Theory's isGlobalNorm_iff_isLocalNormEverywhere.

items.name: Weak approximation in Q
items.statement: Finitely many p-adic and real conditions on an element of Q can be met simultaneously: Q is dense in ∏_{v∈S} Q_v for every finite set S of places (used throughout: Proposition 6, Remark 8(a), Lemmas 13 and 14). Only weak approximation is used; no strong approximation argument appears.
items.note: At the Tau Ceti pin f790474, TauCeti/NumberTheory/NumberField/Global/Approximation/Weak.lean:202 proves Artin–Whaples weak approximation for any number field at finitely many finite places (adic completions) and infinite places (InfinitePlace.Completion). Take K = ℚ; the adapter identifying these completions with ℚ_p and ℝ is routine. Corrected by REV-PAPER-KOENIGSMANN-16 from planned (GlobalQuadraticForms layer 4 consumes this declaration).

items.name: Observation 0
items.statement: If Z is existentially definable in Q, then it is also universally definable: Q \ Z = {x | ∃m, n, a, b ∈ Z: n ≠ 0, ±1, am + bn = 1, m = xn} is then diophantine.

items.name: Theorem 1: Z is universally definable in Q
items.statement: There is n ≥ 1 and g ∈ Z[t; x₁, …, x_n] such that for every t ∈ Q: t ∈ Z iff ∀x₁ … ∀x_n ∈ Q, g(t; x₁, …, x_n) ≠ 0. Moreover no quantifier-free formula defines Z in Q.

items.name: Corollary 2 and 2′: Q \ Z is diophantine
items.statement: Q \ Z is diophantine in Q; equivalently there is an affine variety V over Q and a morphism π: V → A¹ with π(V(Q)) = Q \ Z.

items.name: Corollary 3 and 3′: Th_∀∃(Q) is undecidable
items.statement: The set of true ∀∃-sentences of Q in L_ring is undecidable; equivalently no algorithm decides, for a Q-morphism π: V → W of affine varieties, whether V(Q) → W(Q) is surjective.
items.note: Use the Diophantine syntax and substitution framework of items 46 and 42 and LD.0; this unconditional universal-existential transfer must retain its own quantifier-prefix proof using the universal definition of Z. It does not assume the still-open existential definition in item 48. Item 49 owns the general existential transfer when a Diophantine subring is actually given.

items.name: Quaternion trace sets S_{a,b}, T_{a,b} and Δ_{a,b}
items.statement: For a, b ∈ Q^×: Δ_{a,b} ⊆ P ∪ {∞} is the set of places where H_{a,b} ⊗ Q_p ≇ M₂(Q_p); S_{a,b} = {2x₁ | ∃x₂, x₃, x₄: x₁² − ax₂² − bx₃² + abx₄² = 1} (traces of norm-one elements); T_{a,b} = S_{a,b} + S_{a,b}; S_{a,b}(Q_p), T_{a,b}(Q_p) likewise over Q_p (T differs from Poonen's by omitting {0, …, 2309}).
items.note: Reuse item 6: S_{a,b} = {2 * x.re : x in QuaternionAlgebra Q a 0 b, QuaternionAlgebra.normForm a 0 b x = 1}. The pinned normForm, normForm_apply_coordinates and equivalent_normForm_weightedSumSquares give exactly the displayed norm equation. The sets S, T, their local versions and their arithmetic properties remain missing; the underlying norm form is built.

items.name: Poonen's local facts (a), (b), (d) and Fact (c)
items.statement: (a) p ∉ Δ_{a,b} ⇒ S_{a,b}(Q_p) = Q_p; (b) p ∈ Δ_{a,b} ⇒ φ_p^{-1}(U_p) ⊆ S_{a,b}(Q_p) ⊆ Z_p, where U_p = {s ∈ F_p | x² − sx + 1 irreducible over F_p}; (c) S_{a,b}(R) = R if a > 0 or b > 0, and [−2, 2] if a, b < 0; (d) F_p = U_p + U_p for p > 11. (U₂ = {1}, U₃ = {0}, U₅ = {1,4}, U₇ = {0,3,4}, U₁₁ = {0,1,5,6,10}.)

items.name: Proposition 6: T_{a,b} = ∩_{p ∈ Δ_{a,b}} Z_(p)
items.statement: For a, b ∈ Q^×, T_{a,b} = ∩_{p ∈ Δ_{a,b}} Z_(p), where Z_(∞) := {x ∈ Q : −4 ≤ x ≤ 4} and an empty intersection is Q.
items.locator: §2, Proposition 6 and proof, pp. 76–78 (with the table for p = 2 corrected, E1)

items.name: A ∀∃-definition of Z with a degree-8 polynomial (Poonen's Theorem 4.1, simplified)
items.statement: Z = ∩_{l ∈ P} Z_(l) = ∩_{a,b>0} T_{a,b}; hence t ∈ Z iff ∀a, b ∃x₁, …, x₄, y₂, y₃, y₄: (a + Σxᵢ²)(b + Σxᵢ²)[(x₁² − ax₂² − bx₃² + abx₄² − 1)² + ((t − 2x₁)² − 4ay₂² − 4by₃² + 4aby₄² − 4)²] = 0. The paper states that this lowers the degree of Poonen's polynomial from 9244 to 8: the polynomial has degree 8 in the quantified variables x₁, …, x₄, y₂, y₃, y₄ (total degree 12 when a, b and t are counted).

items.name: The existentially defined rings R^{[k]}_p and R^{[1]}_{p,q}
items.statement: For p, q ∈ Q^×: R^{[3]}_p = T_{−1,−p} + T_{2,−p}; R^{[5]}_p = T_{−2,−p} + T_{2,−p}; R^{[7]}_p = T_{−1,−p} + T_{−2,p}; R^{[1]}_{p,q} = T_{−2p,q} + T_{2p,q}. These are uniformly diophantine in the parameters.

items.name: Remark 8(a): sums of T-sets
items.statement: For a, b, c, d ∈ Q^× with at least one positive, T_{a,b} + T_{c,d} = ∩_{l ∈ Δ_{a,b} ∩ Δ_{c,d}} Z_(l).

items.name: Prime sets P^{[k]}, P(p), P^{[k]}(p), P(p, q)
Proposition 10: identification of the R-rings
items.statement: (a) Z_(2) = T_{3,3} + T_{2,5}. (b) For k = 3, 5, 7 and p ∈ Q^×: R^{[k]}_p = ∩_{l ∈ P^{[k]}(p)} Z_(l) if p ≡ k (mod 8Z_(2)), and otherwise either this or ∩_{l ∈ P^{[k]}(p) ∪ {2}} Z_(l); in particular R^{[k]}_p = Z_(p) for a prime p ≡ k mod 8. (c) For p ≡ 1, q ≡ 3 (mod 8Z_(2)), R^{[1]}_{p,q} = ∩_{l ∈ P(p,q)} Z_(l); in particular R^{[1]}_{p,q} = Z_(p) for primes p ≡ 1, q ≡ 3 mod 8 with (p/q) = −1.
items.locator: §2, Proposition 10 and proof, pp. 80–81 (proof misprints E2)

items.name: Corollary 11: an ∀∃-definition through the R-rings
The sets T^×_{a,b}, I^c_{a,b} and J_{a,b}
items.statement: T^×_{a,b} = {u ∈ T_{a,b} | ∃v ∈ T_{a,b}, uv = 1}; I^c_{a,b} = c·Q²·T^×_{a,b} ∩ (1 − Q²·T^×_{a,b}); J_{a,b} = (I^a_{a,b} + I^a_{a,b}) ∩ (I^b_{a,b} + I^b_{a,b}); {(a, b, x) | x ∈ J_{a,b}} is diophantine.

items.name: Lemma 13: T^×, I^c and J explicitly
items.statement: (a) T^×_{a,b} = ∩_{l∈Δ_{a,b}} Z^×_(l) if ∞ ∉ Δ_{a,b}, and ([−4, −1/4] ∪ [1/4, 4]) ∩ ∩_{l ∈ Δ_{a,b} \ {∞}} Z^×_(l) otherwise; (b) I^c_{a,b} = {0} ∪ {y ∈ Q^× | v_l(y) odd and positive for l ∈ Δ_{a,b} ∩ P(c), v_l(y), v_l(1 − y) even for l ∈ Δ_{a,b} \ (P(c) ∪ {∞})}; (c) I^c_{a,b} + I^c_{a,b} = ∩_{l ∈ Δ_{a,b} ∩ P(c)} lZ_(l); (d) J_{a,b} = ∩_{l∈Δ} lZ_(l) with Δ = Δ_{a,b} \ {2, ∞} if 2 ∈ Δ_{a,b} and v₂(a), v₂(b) are even, and Δ_{a,b} \ {∞} otherwise. In particular, when ∞ ∉ Δ_{a,b}, T^× is the unit group of T_{a,b}; if moreover Δ_{a,b} ≠ ∅ and (2 ∉ Δ_{a,b} or v₂(a) or v₂(b) is odd), J_{a,b} is the Jacobson radical of T_{a,b} (the printed text omits Δ_{a,b} ≠ ∅, E5).

items.name: Lemma 14: Jacobson radicals of sums
items.statement: For a, b, c, d ∈ Q^×, one positive, Δ := Δ_{a,b} ∩ Δ_{c,d} ∌ 2 and R = ∩_{l∈Δ} Z_(l): J_{a,b} + J_{c,d} = ∩_{l∈Δ} lZ_(l); if Δ ≠ ∅ this is J(R).

items.name: Corollary 15: the sets Φ_k and Ψ, and diophantine Jacobson radicals
items.statement: Φ_k = {p ∈ Q_{>0} | p ≡ k (mod 8Z_(2)), P(p) ⊆ P^{[1]} ∪ P^{[k]}}, Ψ = {(p, q) ∈ Φ₁ × Φ₃ | p ∈ 2(Q^×)²(1 + J(R^{[3]}_q))}. (a) Φ_k is diophantine; (b) for k = 3, 5, 7 and p ∈ Φ_k: P^{[k]}(p) ≠ ∅ and {0} ≠ J(R^{[k]}_p) = J_{−1,−p} + J_{2,−p}, J_{−2,−p} + J_{2,−p}, J_{−1,−p} + J_{−2,p} respectively, uniformly diophantine in p; (c) Ψ is diophantine.

items.name: Proposition 16: the case p ∈ Φ₁
items.statement: For (p, q) ∈ Ψ: (a) P(p, q) ≠ ∅; (b) J(R^{[1]}_{p,q}) = J_{−2p,q} + J_{2p,q}; (c) {(p, q, x) | (p, q) ∈ Ψ, x ∈ J(R^{[1]}_{p,q})} is diophantine.

items.name: Lemma 17: from existential to universal
items.statement: For a semilocal R = ∩_{l∈Δ} Z_(l) ⊆ Q (Δ finite) let R̃ = {x ∈ Q | ¬∃y ∈ J(R), xy = 1}. (a) If J(R) is diophantine then R̃ is universally definable; (b) R̃ = ∪_{l∈Δ} Z_(l) if Δ ≠ ∅; (c) R̃ = R for R = Z_(p).

items.name: Proposition 18: the universal definition
Definition 19 and Lemma 20: the sets S_p
items.statement: For p ∈ Φ₁, S_p = {x | ∃q: (p, q) ∈ Ψ, q ∈ (R^{[1]}_{p,q})^×, x ∈ R^{[1]}_{p,q}}. (a) S_p is diophantine; (b) S_p = ∪_{l ∈ P(p)} Z_(l) (∅ if p is a square); (c) S_p = Z_(p) for a prime p ≡ 1 mod 8.

items.name: Proposition 21(a): disjointness of prime sets is diophantine
items.statement: For fixed k ∈ {3, 5, 7}, the property 'x, y ∈ Φ_k and P^{[k]}(x) ∩ P^{[k]}(y) = ∅' is diophantine.

items.name: Proposition 21(b): non-squares are diophantine (elementary proof)
items.statement: The set Q \ Q² (restricted to Q^×) is diophantine: x ∉ Q² iff x < 0, or v₂(x) is odd, or ∃p ∈ Φ₃ with x ∈ 2·(Q^×)²·(1 + J(R^{[3]}_p)).
items.locator: §3, Proposition 21(b) and proof, p. 88 (misprint E3); also [Poo09b]

items.name: Proposition 21(c): 'x ≡ k and x ∉ Φ_k' is diophantine
items.statement: For fixed k ∈ {1, 3, 5, 7}, the property 'x ≡ k (mod 8Z_(2)) and x ∉ Φ_k' is diophantine.

items.name: Proposition 21(d): 'P^{[k]}(x) = ∅' is diophantine
items.statement: For fixed k ∈ {3, 5, 7}, the property P^{[k]}(x) = ∅ is diophantine.
items.note: The proof's displayed identity is false as printed (E6). The corrected one, {x ∈ Q^× : P^{[3]}(x) = ∅} = {±1, ±2}·(Q^×)²·Φ′₅Φ′₅·Φ′₇Φ′₇ with Φ′_k = Φ_k ∪ {1}, still exhibits the set as diophantine; similarly for k = 5, 7.

items.name: Proposition 21(e): non-norms from quadratic fields are diophantine
items.statement: The set of (x, y) ∈ (Q^×)² with x ∉ N(y), the image of the norm Q(√y) → Q, is diophantine (explicit formula with a₃ = a₅ = 2, a₇ = −1).

items.name: Corollary 22: an ∀∃-definition with one universal quantifier
items.statement: For t ∈ Q: t ∈ Z iff ∀p (t ∈ Z_(2) ∧ (p ∈ Q²·(2 + 4Z_(2)) ∨ ⋁_{k=1,3,5,7}(p ≠ 0 ∧ p ∈ Q²·(k + 8Z_(2)) ∧ (p ∉ Φ_k ∨ p ∈ Q² ∨ (p ∈ Φ_k \ Q² ∧ t ∈ R_k(p)))))), where R_k(p) = R^{[k]}_p for k = 3, 5, 7 and R_1(p) = S_p (the printed formula writes R^{[k]}_p also for k = 1, E4).

items.name: The model-theoretic criterion for existential definability of Z
items.statement: Z is diophantine in Q iff for all models Q* ⊆ Q** of Th(Q) (as L_ring-substructures) the rings of integers satisfy Z* ⊆ Z** ([PD11, Lemma 3.1.6]).
items.note: Mathlib has elementary embeddings and substructures (FirstOrder.Language.ElementaryEmbedding) and the easy direction of the criterion, that existential formulas are preserved upward along embeddings (FirstOrder.Language.BoundedFormula.IsExistential.realize_embedding), but not the converse preservation theorem.

items.name: Proposition 23: closure properties of models of Th(Q)
items.statement: For models Q* ⊆ Q** of Th(Q) with rings of integers Z*, Z**: (a) Z** ∩ Q* ⊆ Z*; (b) Z** ∩ Q* is integrally closed in Q*; (c) (Q**)ⁿ ∩ Q* = (Q*)ⁿ for all n (via [CTVG14]); (d) if Z is diophantine in Q then Z** ∩ Q* = Z* and Q* is algebraically closed in Q**.
items.note: Part (a) is the universal formula of Theorem 1 pulled back along Q* ⊆ Q** (compare Mathlib's FirstOrder.Language.BoundedFormula.IsUniversal.realize_embedding); (c) consumes the Colliot-Thélène–Van Geel theorem explicitly itemized as item 45; (d) needs MRDP (item 2). It is routed with Theorem 1 at LD.4 for that reason.

items.name: Remark 24: Th(Q) is not model complete
items.statement: There are models Q* ⊆ Q** of Th(Q) with Q* not existentially closed in Q**, because not every definable subset of Q is diophantine (an undecidable r.e. set has a definable, non-diophantine complement).
items.note: Uses the definitions and model-completeness criterion in items 43–44 (LD.0), the Q-specific existential/Diophantine equivalence and recursive enumerability in item 42, and MRDP/item 2. LD.0 → LD.4 is the existing dependency direction; this consequence remains in LD.4.

items.name: Diophantine closure operations over rings, with domain and Q specializations
items.statement: For a commutative ring R with 1, use item 46: subsets of R^n defined by finite polynomial systems with existential witnesses are closed under finite intersections, coordinate projection and polynomial preimage. If R is a Diophantine unital subring of S, every Diophantine subset of R^n is Diophantine in S^n by constraining both free coordinates and all witnesses to R; thus such definitions compose. Over an integral domain, finite unions are Diophantine (use a selector e with e(e-1)=0, e f_i=0 and (1-e) g_j=0). Over Q, a finite conjunction reduces to a single equation by a sum of squares; over a field, nonzero is Diophantine via xy=1; over Q, nonnegative is Diophantine via four squares. These Q clauses make every existential ring formula over Q Diophantine. Over a computable ring with an effective enumeration, decidable equality and computable ring operations and coefficients, each such Diophantine set is recursively enumerable.
items.locator: used throughout: Step 1 formula p. 79, Remark 8(b), Definition 12, Corollary 15(a), Propositions 16(c), 21, Remark 24
items.note: The general ring operations are the common LD.4 owner for PAPER-ALPOGE-BHARGAVA-SHNIDMAN-26/46 and /47; its /1 uses the carrier in item 46 and /3 uses the transfer in item 49. The revised Part II imports all four foundations. The arbitrary-ring generalization is an explicit elementary extension of the paper’s Q argument, also supplying MRS Lemmas 4.3 and 4.5; it is not asserted to be printed in Koenigsmann. Finite unions are deliberately restricted to integral domains: in R = F_2 × F_2 every existential conjunction of polynomial equations factors componentwise, whereas {0_R,1_R} does not. Thus the union of the two Diophantine singleton sets need not be Diophantine over a general ring under the finite-system definition. The single-equation sum-of-squares reduction is only asserted over Q (or formally real fields), not all fields.

items.name: Existentially closed substructures and model-complete theories
items.statement: For an L-substructure M of N, M is existentially closed in N if each existential L-formula with parameters from M that holds in N already holds in M. A first-order L-theory T is model complete if every embedding between models of T is elementary. The equivalence with all such inclusions being existentially closed is the theorem in item 44, not part of the definition.
items.note: Build on Mathlib FirstOrder.Language.ElementaryEmbedding and FirstOrder.Language.BoundedFormula.IsExistential at 082e2d3. These bases do not define model completeness or existential closedness. This is LD.0 work, consumed by item 41.

api.name: FirstOrder.Language.IsExistentiallyClosed
api.statement: Predicate on a specified structure embedding, with parameters pulled along that embedding.

api.name: FirstOrder.Language.Theory.IsModelComplete
api.statement: Every embedding between models of T preserves and reflects every formula.

api.name: FirstOrder.Language.IsExistentiallyClosed.of_elementaryEmbedding
api.statement: An elementary embedding reflects existential formulas, hence is existentially closed.

unitTests.name: existentiallyClosed_identity
unitTests.statement: The identity embedding is existentially closed.

unitTests.name: real_complex_not_existentiallyClosed
unitTests.statement: The ring embedding ℝ into ℂ is not existentially closed: X^2+1 has a root in ℂ and none in ℝ. This tests the embedding predicate, not two models of a common theory.

items.name: Model completeness, existential closedness and existential normal forms
items.statement: For a first-order theory T, the following are equivalent: every embedding between models of T is elementary; every model of T is existentially closed in every model of T extending it; every formula is equivalent modulo T to an existential formula. In particular a definable subset of a model of a model-complete T, with a fixed finite parameter tuple, has an existential definition using that tuple.
items.locator: Section 4, p. 92, paragraph before Remark 24 and its proof; general preservation input on p. 91 ([PD11, Lemma 3.1.6])
items.note: Missing general model-theoretic theorem, routed to LD.0 with items 39 and 43. The easy upward preservation direction has Mathlib FirstOrder.Language.BoundedFormula.IsExistential.realize_embedding; compactness/preservation and the model-completeness criterion still require a blueprint proof. Do not confuse this with Mathlib model_completeTheory, which merely says a structure models its own complete theory.

items.name: Colliot-Thélène–Van Geel: non-n-th powers are Diophantine
items.statement: For every number field K and integer n >= 1, the set {x in K : there is no y in K with y^n=x} is Diophantine in K. For n > 1 this is equivalently K^× minus the n-th powers in K^×; 0 is an n-th power. For n=1 the set is empty.
items.locator: Section 3, p. 90; proof of Proposition 23(c), pp. 91–92 ([CTVG14]); independently checked arXiv:1401.0915v1, Theorem 4.3, pp. 16–17
items.note: External theorem input for item 40(c), not a consequence of the elementary n=2 proof. LD.4 takes Colliot-Thélène–Van Geel as an additional source and closes its proof and Brauer–Manin dependencies in its blueprint, importing their owners. Per PROTOCOL section 16, this cited result is one extraction item; its proof is not re-extracted here.

items.name: Diophantine subsets of finite powers of a commutative ring
items.statement: For a commutative ring R with 1 and n >= 0, a subset D of R^n is Diophantine if there are finitely many witness variables and finitely many polynomials f_i over R such that x belongs to D exactly when some witness tuple y in R satisfies f_i(x,y)=0 for every i. Coefficients and parameter sets are explicit. This finite-system notion is separate from arbitrary existential ring formulas and from reduction to one equation.
items.locator: General carrier needed for item 42 and PAPER-ALPOGE-BHARGAVA-SHNIDMAN-26/1; Mazur–Rubin–Shlapentokh arXiv:2208.09963v3, Definition 2.2, p. 5; Koenigsmann Section 1, p. 73, Q specialization
items.note: Owned once by LD.4, with logical syntax imported from LD.0. Mathlib Dioph is over natural-number tuples, not this ring-general carrier. Reuse the exact carrier in the ABS Part II; its existing /1 API is a consumer specification, not a second definition. The broad ring statement is stated as a common generalization, not attributed verbatim to Koenigsmann.

api.name: DiophantineSet.exists_iff
api.statement: Membership iff the chosen finite system has a witness tuple.

api.name: DiophantineSet.polynomial_zeroSet
api.statement: A finite polynomial zero locus is Diophantine with no extra witnesses.

api.name: DiophantineSet.map_ringEquiv
api.statement: A ring equivalence transports coefficients, witnesses and the defined subset; transport along identities and composites agrees.

api.name: DiophantineSet.intersection
api.statement: Concatenate finite systems and disjoint witness tuples; the theorem is item 42.

unitTests.name: diophantine_units
unitTests.statement: The unit subset is given by xy=1; over Z this excludes 2, so it is not the nonzero subset.

unitTests.name: diophantine_zero_arity
unitTests.statement: At n=0 a system records solvability as a subset of the singleton R^0. An empty system defines the whole singleton.

unitTests.name: diophantine_product_union_failure
unitTests.statement: In F_2 × F_2, {0_R} and {1_R} are Diophantine, but their union is not definable by an existential finite polynomial system: such solution projections factor as products.

items.name: Local square criterion over Q_p
items.statement: For an odd prime p and u in Z_p^×, u is a square in Q_p iff its reduction in F_p^× is a square; in particular 1+pZ_p consists of squares in Q_p^×. Also 1+8Z_2 consists of squares in Q_2^×.
items.locator: Section 2, p. 78 (dyadic table); Section 3, proofs of Lemma 20(b) and Proposition 21(b), pp. 87–88
items.note: LocalFieldsRamification Layer 1 owns the local power and sharp dyadic-square interfaces; QuadraticFormInvariants 6A consumes them. Mathlib hensels_lemma is a base, not the complete stated square criterion: for X^2-u the residual-root case has unit derivative when p is odd, while u in 1+8Z_2 gives |1-u|_2 < |2|_2^2 at 1. The sharp dyadic theorem is absent at the pin; no library status is claimed for the combined item.

items.name: Conditional existential undecidability of Q from a Diophantine Z
items.statement: If Z is Diophantine in Q, then the existential ring theory of Q is undecidable, and Hilbert’s tenth problem over Q has a negative answer. Relativize every integer variable to the fixed Diophantine definition of Z and apply MRDP.
items.note: The Q instance of the shared transfer in item 49, using item 42 to identify finite systems with the usual existential/single-equation formulation. The hypothesis that Z is Diophantine in Q is not claimed proved.

items.name: Transfer of undecidability along a Diophantine integer subring
items.statement: Let R be a commutative ring with an injective unital map Z → R and a fixed finite polynomial system over R defining its image. Then solvability of finite polynomial systems over R is undecidable, with inputs given by finite expressions in the integer coefficients and the finitely many constants of that definition (or any effective coefficient presentation containing them). Replace each integer variable by an R-variable constrained by the defining system to reduce integer polynomial solvability to R-system solvability. A reduction from systems to one equation requires a separate hypothesis/theorem.
items.locator: Koenigsmann Section 1, p. 73 (Q case); Mazur–Rubin–Shlapentokh arXiv:2208.09963v3, Proposition 2.3(1) and proof, p. 5 (general ring form)
items.note: LD.4 is the single owner, shared with PAPER-ALPOGE-BHARGAVA-SHNIDMAN-26/3. The latter Part II imports this interpretation theorem, item 46 and item 42; it supplies its separate number-ring and single-equation adapters. This theorem does not presume an effective presentation of every abstract ring.

routes.reason: LD.4 is the atlas's layer for Diophantine definability and undecidability, and its specification asks that other-field variants be recorded individually rather than copied from the integers. Koenigsmann's universal definition of Z in Q (with Robinson's and Poonen's ∀∃-definitions as predecessors), the diophantine sets it produces (Q \ Z, non-squares, non-norms), and the undecidability of Th_∀∃(Q) are exactly such a variant. Its inputs are already planned or built: explicit Hilbert symbols, Hilbert reciprocity, quaternion splitting and local Hilbert symbols in Tau Ceti's QuadraticFormInvariants (layer 2 and 6C), Hasse–Minkowski and local–global norms in Tau Ceti's GlobalQuadraticForms (layers 4 and 6), weak approximation in Tau Ceti itself (TauCeti.GlobalNumberFields.weakApproximation_denseRange), and MRDP in LD.4 itself. The paper-specific material — the quaternion trace sets S_{a,b}, T_{a,b} with Poonen's local lemmas, the R-rings, the existential Jacobson radicals and the existential-to-universal step — is elementary and belongs with its only consumer, so a separate roadmap is not warranted. The §4 results that use Theorem 1 or MRDP — Proposition 23 (whose (a) is Theorem 1 read in models and whose (d) uses MRDP) and Remark 24 (r.e. sets) — are routed here too, since LD.4 already requires LD.0; routing them to LD.0 would make LD.0 depend on LD.4. (Moved from route 2 by REV-PAPER-KOENIGSMANN-16.) Explicit mandatory supplier imports for the LD.4 blueprint are tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/QuadraticFormInvariants#layer-2-quaternion-algebras-and-the-four-fold-splitting-criterion, tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/QuadraticFormInvariants#6c-the-hilbert-symbol-and-the-local-hasse-invariant, tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/GlobalQuadraticForms#layer-4-global-square-norm-and-approximation-lemmas, tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/GlobalQuadraticForms#layer-6-representation-and-isometry. The first two supply items 7–9 at their stated scopes; the global layers supply items 8–10, including the archimedean symbol and local-global adapters. Item 11 reuses tauceti:TauCeti.GlobalNumberFields.weakApproximation_denseRange directly. These are import requirements recorded in this route, not existing stage edges: the fixes report requests the four links from the maintainer because link files are outside this issue’s deliverables. Item 47 also imports tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/LocalFieldsRamification#layer-1-units-the-filtration-and-the-multiplicative-group for local square criteria. LD.4 owns the general ring Diophantine carrier (46), closure/composition API (42) and interpretation transfer (49), which the ABS Part II consumes rather than rebuilds. The external non-n-th-power theorem (45) is a separate deep input and needs its own source proof in the LD.4 blueprint.

Section 4 opens with the general preservation criterion: a definable set is existentially definable modulo a complete theory iff it is preserved upward along inclusions of models ([PD11, Lemma 3.1.6]), specialized to Z in Q. That is model theory of elementary extensions and substructures, which LD.0 (languages, structures, definable sets, elementary extensions) owns, with Mathlib's ElementaryEmbedding, ElementarySubstructure and IsExistential.realize_embedding as its library base. Proposition 23 and Remark 24 depend on Theorem 1 and MRDP and are routed with them to LD.4 (moved by REV-PAPER-KOENIGSMANN-16). Items 43–44 add existentially closed embeddings, model-complete theories and the existential normal-form criterion; item 41 imports these through the existing LD.0 → LD.4 edge.

sourceIssues.reason: Take a = b = 1. Then H_{1,1} ≅ M₂(Q) splits everywhere, ∆_{1,1} = ∅, T_{1,1} = Q by Proposition 6, and by Lemma 13(d) with the paper's convention that an empty intersection is Q, J_{1,1} = Q (directly: T^× = Q^×, so Q²·T^× = Q and I^c = Q). But the Jacobson radical of the field Q is {0}. Lemma 14 states its own 'In particular' only for ∆ ≠ ∅, and Corollary 15 and Proposition 16 use Lemma 14 with ∆ = P^{[k]}(p) or P(p, q), which they prove nonempty; so no argument after Lemma 13 is affected.

sourceIssues.locator: Proof of Proposition 21(d), displayed identities, p. 89 (published version only; arXiv v2, p. 19, argues with an explicit formula in y₁, …, y₈ instead)
sourceIssues.printed: The source defines Pk to comprise all finite products of primes belonging to P[k] ∪ P[1]. It asserts Pk · (Q×)² = Φ′kΦ′k. It then gives {x : P[3](x) = ∅} = {1, −1, 2, −2}P1P5P7 = ⋃_{k=1,5,7} Φ′kΦ′k.
sourceIssues.correction: {x ∈ Q× : P[3](x) = ∅} = {1, −1, 2, −2}·(Q×)²·Φ′5Φ′5·Φ′7Φ′7 (a product, not a union; Φ′1Φ′1 is not needed), and Pk·(Q×)² = (Q×)²·Φ′kΦ′k. This set is still diophantine, so Proposition 21(d) holds.
sourceIssues.reason: The union is wrong: x = 35 = 5·7 has P[3](35) = ∅, but every element of Φ′kΦ′k is positive with all its odd-valuation primes in P[1] ∪ P[k], so 35 lies in none of Φ′1Φ′1, Φ′5Φ′5, Φ′7Φ′7; nor do −1 and 2. The first equality also drops the square factor that the preceding sentence mentions (9 has P[3](9) = ∅ but is not in {±1, ±2}P1P5P7), and Pk·(Q×)² ∋ 4 while every element of Φ′kΦ′k is a 2-adic unit. The corrected identity holds: write x = ε·2^e·z²·m5·m7 with m5 a product of distinct primes from P[1] ∪ P[5] and m7 from P[7]; m5 is in Φ′5Φ′5 up to squares (one factor if the number of P[5]-primes is odd, two if it is even and positive, and m5 = (5m5)·5/5² if it is zero), and likewise m7.
